claims.text: The target system consists of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements.
The relevant synthesis regime uses peak temperatures of approximately 2000 K and cooling rates of approximately 10^5–10^4 K/s.
Single-phase solid-solution formation is governed by competition between atomic-diffusion kinetics during cooling and thermodynamic mixing enthalpies.
Distinct interelement mixing enthalpies create preferences for particular structures.
Limited atomic mobility competes with thermodynamic structural preferences.
A controlled cooling-rate ramp at a critical stage will increase the time available for atomic redistribution.
A temporary diffusion moderator could enhance effective atomic diffusion during synthesis.
High peak temperature provides sufficient atomic mixing for multielement nanoparticles.
Cooling too quickly can cause elemental segregation or phase separation because insufficient time is available for diffusion.
Slower cooling will allow atoms to overcome thermodynamic driving forces that favor phase separation.
Enhanced atomic diffusion will mitigate elemental segregation and promote a homogeneous single-phase structure.
Relative to standard rapid cooling, the controlled cooling intervention will increase phase purity.
Relative to standard rapid cooling, the controlled cooling intervention will reduce elemental segregation.
Relative to standard rapid cooling, the controlled cooling intervention will improve particle-shape uniformity.
Rapid heating and cooling can produce a non-equilibrium single solid solution by suppressing secondary-phase formation.
The cooling intervention may be less effective when intrinsic mixing enthalpies are too large.
The cooling intervention may be less effective when atomic-size differences are too large.

contradictions.description: The mechanism and baseline portray rapid cooling as diffusion-limited and segregation-promoting, whereas the boundary also states that rapid cooling suppresses secondary phases and preserves a single solid solution. The hypothesis does not define the cooling-rate window that reconciles these opposing roles.
